title: Baba Buddha
hook: the boy Nanak met lived to serve six Gurus and, tradition says, applied the tilak to their successors

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Khivi, named in the Granth: shade like a leafy tree, kheer made with ghee. Your line was generous kitchen. Did something you made go a little further? Day eight hundred six.

A boy is out with the cattle when a holy man passes by on the road. He could have kept his eyes on the herd. Instead he brings milk, sits down, and asks a question that sounds far too old for him. How do I escape death? The holy man looks at him and asks why a boy so young is thinking about that. The boy's answer, as Sikhs tell it, earned him a new name for the rest of his life. Today: Baba Buddha.
screen: `A BOY WITH THE CATTLE.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT DEATH.` → `AN ANSWER THAT EARNED A NAME.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Sikh tradition, and it goes like this. The boy, named Bura, tells Guru Nanak what he saw at home. When his mother lights the cooking fire, she doesn't start with the big logs. She starts with the small twigs, and they burn up first. So, he says, if the small ones go first in the fire, who's to say death will wait for the old? Guru Nanak, the story says, answered that he spoke like an old man, a buddha, a wise elder. And the name stuck: Baba Buddha. Then comes the long part. That boy, tradition says, lived to serve six Gurus, from Guru Nanak on. When guruship passed from one Guru to the next, tradition says it was Baba Buddha who applied the tilak, the mark on the forehead, to the new Guru. The same pair of hands that once herded cattle by the road marked Guru after Guru, across a lifetime. And Sikh tradition remembers him at the Harmandir Sahib too: when Guru Arjan installed the Granth there, tradition says Baba Buddha was asked to read from it. Through all of it, the stories don't make him a leader who sought power. He's honored for service. He tended, he read, he marked, he stayed. His question as a boy was how to escape death. The name came first, from a boy watching twigs catch in his mother's fire. The long life of service came after, and Sikhs remember the two together: a child who spoke like an elder, and an elder who kept serving like that same attentive boy, one Guru after another.
screen: `SMALL TWIGS BURN FIRST.` · `A BOY CALLED BUDDHA: A WISE ELDER.` · `THE TILAK, GURU AFTER GURU.` · `HONORED FOR SERVICE, NOT POWER.` · then, large: `SIX GURUS SERVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve for the long haul. In the sit, bring to mind one thing you could keep doing for a long time: a weekly call, a small job at a gurdwara or a community place, a way you help at home. Not something heroic. Something you could still be doing years from now. Hold it with each breath, and let it feel ordinary. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Baba Buddha. The boy whose question about death earned him the name of a wise elder, and who, tradition says, served six Gurus and marked their successors with the tilak.
Your line: six gurus served. Today, do the one small service you could keep doing for years, and do it once with care. Day eight hundred six.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Baba Buddha as a model of lifelong seva, and gurdwaras connected with his memory, including Gurdwara Bir Baba Buddha Sahib, draw visitors who come to remember his service.

fork.setup: you're the boy with the cattle, and Guru Nanak asks why someone so young is thinking about death. what do you say?
options: that you heard the elders talking.
that small twigs burn up first in your mother's fire.
that you're afraid of the dark.
fork.reveal: in the story he points to the cooking fire, and Guru Nanak says he speaks like a wise elder, a buddha.

original.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service, which Baba Buddha is remembered for.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man in Sikh history.
what it means: a boy whose question about death earned him the name of a wise elder, and whose life became long service to the Gurus.
what a scholar hears: the twig story, the tilak and the reading at Harmandir Sahib come from Sikh tradition, not from the Granth's own text.

notes: 'Six Gurus' and 'from Guru Nanak on' follow the index line; the claim is framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm the count.
The twig story and the boy's birth name Bura: traditional; confirm.
Tradition that Baba Buddha was asked to read from the Granth at its installation at Harmandir Sahib: confirm wording (many sources call him the first granthi; the script avoids the superlative).
howItsDone mentions Gurdwara Bir Baba Buddha Sahib: confirm name.
'Buddha' glossed as a wise elder / old one: confirm.
Editor pass: hook no longer claims 'a very long life' or a question 'no child is supposed to ask'; cut stock lines 'Here's what makes his life remarkable' and 'Think about what that means'.

Audit (2026-10-01): ending no longer says he was called wise 'because the service was long', which contradicted the story told in the same teach (Guru Nanak named him for the twig answer); also dropped the narrator's moral 'give a whole life to something larger'.
